questions.q: What is a major reason Linux dominates public cloud VM and container images over Windows?
options: The Linux kernel is open source with no per-instance license fee, which matters enormously at cloud scale
Windows cannot run on virtual machines at all
Cloud providers are contractually forbidden from offering Windows images
Linux requires more hardware resources, which cloud providers prefer
questions.explain: A fleet of thousands of Linux VMs costs nothing in OS licensing, while the same fleet of Windows Server VMs pays a license fee on every instance.

questions.q: Which package manager is used by the Debian/Ubuntu distro family?
options: apt / apt-get
yum / dnf
npm
chmod
questions.explain: Debian and Ubuntu use apt (and the older apt-get); RHEL-family distros use yum or dnf instead.

questions.q: What is Amazon Linux, and why does it matter?
options: AWS's own RHEL-derived distro, purpose-built for EC2 and often the default AMI there
A Windows-only distro exclusive to Azure
A graphical desktop environment, not a server distro
An outdated distro no longer used on AWS
questions.explain: Amazon Linux is derived from RHEL conventions and optimized specifically to run well on AWS EC2 instances.

questions.q: Why does a small base image footprint matter specifically for containers?
options: Containers are meant to start in milliseconds and ship as small images, so a minimal OS layer (megabytes, not gigabytes) is essential
Container platforms refuse to run any image larger than 1MB
Footprint size has no real effect on container performance or portability
Larger images always start faster than smaller ones
questions.explain: A minimal Linux base image can be a few megabytes, while a Windows Server Core container image runs into gigabytes — a gap that matters when containers need to start fast.

questions.q: What does the file /etc/os-release tell you on a Linux machine?
options: Which distro and version that machine is running
The current CPU temperature
A list of all installed packages
The machine's public IP address
questions.explain: Running cat /etc/os-release reports fields like NAME, VERSION, and ID, which identify the distro — the fastest way to confirm what OS a given VM is running.
